extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of literature studying poetic aesthetics and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and aesthetic standards for judging and composing different poetic kinds (simple, sentimental, elegiac, idyl/pastoral, didactic, dramatic), with examples and warnings drawn from German and classical poets. Emphasizes balance between sensuous perception and the ideal, form and matter, and legitimate poetic freedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and sensuous immediacy (simple poet)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple poet 'receives the impression of objects with a calm feeling, simple, easy, and to give forth in like manner the impression received.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry of the simple kind depends on immediate sensuous intuition: the poet should present the object itself, not a reflected version of it. Simplicity should be genuine — the soul must be free of artifice and display a horror of cunning or arbitrary fancy. Examples: simple pastoral and truthful landscape portraiture; avoid mediation by abstract reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of introspective spectatorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic warns that in some poets 'the poem does not communicate to us, properly speaking, his feelings, but the thoughts that they suggest to him' — the poet becomes a spectator of his own emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional immediacy is preferable to poetry that turns feeling into object of reflection. If the poet constantly observes and comments on his feelings, the reader's emotion will be less vivid. Anti-pattern: elegies that report reflection ('idea follows fast on idea') rather than first-hand feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic poetry must pass into spiritual intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Didactic poetry treating 'super-sensuous' themes must 'make them pass from the finite to the infinite, and raise them to the state of objects of spiritual intuition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure conceptual or discursive thought cannot thrive as poetry; didactic poems must transform thought into poetic, spiritual intuition (raise to the ideal) rather than remain merely instructive. The author notes few didactic poems successfully make thought itself 'poetic and remain so.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution can redeem non-poetic thought (use of images/ideal flight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when the thought itself is not poetical, 'the execution becomes so sometimes, occasionally by the use of images, at other times by a flight towards the ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A didactic or intellectual subject may be made poetical by imagery or idealizing leaps. Use of images and flights toward the ideal are cited as means to render didactic content poetic (example: parts of Haller's poems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of sensuous and intellectual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic faults poets whose 'sensuous is overweighted by the intellectual' or who 'constantly teaches rather than paints.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem combines spirit and matter — the 'intimate union of spirit with matter' — and should not be overly abstract or merely didactic. Strengths like energy and earnestness are good, but excessive abstraction prevents attainment of beauty. Anti-pattern: works that instruct more than they evoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and concentration into a living whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic traits should 'concentrate to form an individual, without completing each other to make a living whole, without rounding to a form, a figure' is a defect (ascribed to Kleist when failing outside lyrical mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery and traits should cohere and accumulate to mould characters and scenes into determinate, living forms. Rapid succession of brilliant but disconnected traits leads to sportiveness rather than creation; it works in lyric fragments but fails in dramatic/epic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinate forms for dramatic and plastic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: For works representing 'men and human actions' the imagination must be 'kept within certain fixed and necessary limits' and characters must be 'perfectly determinate' for imagination to represent them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic and epic poetry require clearly bounded, determinate characterization and action. Vagueness that might be permissible in musical or lyrical poetry becomes a defect when the object is action or character: characters must be individuals, not mere abstractions or vague types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the imagination with determinate images
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'ought to address' the imagination and 'put before it always perfectly determinate forms,' otherwise the imagination is left too free and the figures lack form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in lofty or ideal subjects (angels, divinities), the poet should supply determinate forms to guide imagination; otherwise the work appeals mainly to the understanding/reflection rather than sensuous imagination (example: parts of the 'Messiah').

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic appeal must refresh sensuous nature as well as intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet 'never calls to arms anything save spirit, without giving recreation and refreshment to sensuous nature by the calm presence of any object' he is less adapted to be a favorite author or guide in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry that appeals only to the intellectual or spiritual faculty (super-sensuous sources) risks being impractical for life; effective poetry balances spiritual elevation with sensuous présence that refreshes the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pervasive sentimentality that enervates
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'constant disposition to this mode of feeling (tender sentimentality) ends necessarily, in the long run, by weakening the character, and makes it fall into a state of passivity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegiac or sentimental poetry should not merely flatter sensuous nature; it must contain an 'energetic and fruitful principle' to enliven subject and produce true beauty. Anti-pattern: excessive tearful melancholy that leads to parody and decay of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral idyl aims to portray innocent, happy humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Idyl 'presents the idea and description of an innocent and happy humanity' — harmony and peace with self and the external world; scene often set in shepherd's cot or infancy of humanity as means, not end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The idyl's purpose is to make the idea of innocence sensuously intuitive; poets may legitimately use pastoral settings as natural means to present this ideal. But they must beware of making the frame the end itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the idyl: intellectual poverty and narrowness
rubrics_metrics.description: By transporting the idyl to 'the time that precedes civilization' it 'loses the advantages thereof' and 'can only inspire us with the sad feeling of a loss, and not the joyous feeling of a hope.' They are 'far too poor for what concerns the mind' and 'their uniform circle is too quickly traversed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idyls have high value for the heart (calming, soothing) but are limited as sustained nourishment for the intellect; they best serve moments of need or calm rather than aim to vivify all faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two routes to ideal value: form vs matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Every kind of poetry can have 'an infinite ideal value' either by giving 'the feeling of the infinite as to form' (absolute representation — simple poetry) or 'as to matter' (idealizing object — sentimental poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should play to their mode's strength: simple poets secure ideal value through perfectly individual, limited representation; sentimental poets must use idealization of matter. Misapplying the other's mode (sentimental poets copying simple objects) risks failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of objects per poetic mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentimental poet 'understands his interests badly when he goes along the trail of the simple poet, and borrows his objects from him' because he thereby imposes limits that he cannot fulfil properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimental poets should choose objects that allow the idealizing treatment appropriate to their mode instead of imitating the simple poet's narrowly circumscribed subjects; failure to match object to mode yields equivocal, unsatisfying work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of poetic freedoms (licenses) depends on nature and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses to transgress conventional decency 'must, therefore, above all, be simplicity' and 'nature only can justify these licenses; whence it follows that you could not legitimately take them up of your own choice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedoms from social decency are permissible only when they derive from natural innocence and are accompanied by unity and consistency of natural effects. They cannot be willfully assumed; the poet must be pure/innocent in soul and consistently reject artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedoms must represent whole humanity, not mere appetites
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful nature alone can justify freedoms; 'they ought not to be a mere outbreak of the appetites... it is from the totality and the fulness of human nature that these vivid manifestations must also issue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When liberties are taken with decency, the work must show other human characteristics that indicate full humanity; if liberties issue merely from sensuous appetites the work is contemptible. Examples: distinction between witty/prosaic voluptuousness and poetic, human simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frigidness and emptiness; the work must be full and human
rubrics_metrics.description: A work is 'common, base, absolutely inexcusable, from the moment it is frigid, and from the moment it is empty' because that shows vulgar appeals or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when taking liberties, the poem must possess warmth, fullness, and humane content. Works that are merely witty or voluptuous without poetic humanity (examples cited: Crebillon, Lacroix, some Voltaire) fail aesthetic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of language and commitment to form
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic notes an equivocal style where 'language floats undecided between poetry and prose, as if he feared either to depart too far from nature, by speaking rhythmical language, or if he completely freed himself from rhythm, to lose all poetic flight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should commit to an appropriate idiom: rhythmical/poetic diction for poetry or freer prose when suitable. A hovering, undecided linguistic mode weakens the work's aesthetic value; avoid indecisive hybrid language.
